claim: DCV is a picorna-like virus assigned to the family Dicistroviridae of the order Picornavirales
source: Among these viruses, DCV, which is a picorna-like virus assigned to the family Dicistroviridae of the order Picornavirales, is a natural pathogen of Drosophila and a classic model virus (Johnson and Christian, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Johnson and Christian, 1998

claim: DCV is a natural pathogen of Drosophila
source: Among these viruses, DCV, which is a picorna-like virus assigned to the family Dicistroviridae of the order Picornavirales, is a natural pathogen of Drosophila and a classic model virus (Johnson and Christian, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Johnson and Christian, 1998

claim: DCV-infected cells showed increased Annexin V and PI staining as infection progressed
source: Consistent with previous study (Lamiable et al., 2016), DCV-infected cells showed increased Annexin V and PI staining as infection progressed when comparing with mock infected cells (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B, and is consistent with a previous study cited (Lamiable et al., 2016)

claim: DCV-infected cells showed an increase in apoptotic cell death by TUNEL staining
source: In this assay, DCV-infected cells also showed an increase in apoptotic cell death comparing with mock infected cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C using TUNEL staining

claim: DCV infection induced RHG gene transcription in Drosophila S2 cells
source: Our data showed that DCV infection induced RHG gene transcription in Drosophila S2 cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The level of reaper mRNA was significantly induced at 6 hr post infection of DCV
source: The level of reaper mRNA was significantly induced at 6 hr post infection (h.p.i) of DCV, while a significant induction of hid or grim mRNA can be detected at 12 h.p.i (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: A significant induction of hid or grim mRNA can be detected at 12 h.p.i of DCV
source: The level of reaper mRNA was significantly induced at 6 hr post infection (h.p.i) of DCV, while a significant induction of hid or grim mRNA can be detected at 12 h.p.i (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: DCV infection is able to induce the transcription of RHG genes and apoptosis in cultured Drosophila cells
source: Altogether, DCV infection is able to induce the transcription of RHG genes and apoptosis in cultured Drosophila cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1

claim: Ectopic expression of DIAP1 effectively inhibited apoptosis
source: Our results showed that the ectopic expression of DIAP1 effectively inhibited apoptosis (Figure 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Ectopic expression of DIAP1 caused about two-fold increase of DCV genomic RNA
source: Our results showed that the ectopic expression of DIAP1 effectively inhibited apoptosis (Figure 2A) and caused about two-fold increase of DCV genomic RNA (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Knockdown of both effector caspases DrICE and DCP1 dramatically inhibited virus-induced apoptosis
source: Moreover, when we knocked down both of the effector caspases DrICE and DCP1, the virus-induced apoptosis was also dramatically inhibited (Figure 2D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Knockdown of both effector caspases DrICE and DCP1 resulted in a significant increase of DCV genomic RNA in infected cells
source: Moreover, when we knocked down both of the effector caspases DrICE and DCP1, the virus-induced apoptosis was also dramatically inhibited (Figure 2D), resulting in a significant increase of DCV genomic RNA in infected cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The inhibition of apoptosis by either DIAP1 overexpression or effector caspases knockdown similarly increased DCV genomic RNA levels in cultured fluids
source: In addition, the inhibition of apoptosis by either DIAP1 overexpression or effector caspases knockdown similarly increased DCV genomic RNA levels in cultured fluids (Figure 2C and F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and F

claim: The loss of p53 function made adult flies more susceptible to viral infection
source: 7 days after the DCV oral infection, almost all p53−/− flies were dead, while about 40% control flies survived in the viral challenge (Figure 2G). These data indicate that the loss of p53 function made adult flies more susceptible to viral infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G

claim: p53−/− flies showed approximately 5-fold increase of DCV genomic RNA at 3 days post DCV oral infection compared with control flies
source: We further tested the DCV genomic RNA level at 3 days post DCV oral infection, and observed approximately 5-fold increase of DCV genomic RNA in p53−/− flies, when comparing with control flies (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H

claim: Apoptosis plays an antiviral role in cultured Drosophila S2 cells and adult flies
source: Taken together, our data show that apoptosis plays an antiviral role in cultured Drosophila S2 cells and adult flies.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 2

claim: DIAP1 has been gradually depleted during the course of DCV infection
source: DIAP1 has been gradually depleted during the course of DCV infection (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Viral infection before CHX addition promoted DIAP1 degradation
source: Although viral infection immediately after CHX addition did not accelerate DIAP1 depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, lanes 1 and 2 vs. 3 and 4), viral infection before CHX addition did promote DIAP1 degradation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, lanes 5 and 6, 1B, 1C, and 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, 1B, 1C, and 1D

claim: DCV infection promotes the degradation of DIAP1, and this process relies on viral protein synthesis and/or viral replication
source: These results show that DCV infection promotes the degradation of DIAP1, and this process relies on viral protein synthesis and/or viral replication, but not the input viral components, as blocking viral protein synthesis eliminated this effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from CHX degradation assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: A slightly smaller, faster-migrating form of endogenous DIAP1 can be detected during DCV infection
source: Intriguingly, a slightly smaller, faster-migrating form of endogenous DIAP1 can be detected (Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The presence of z-VAD-FMK could effectively block the production of the smaller DIAP1
source: Our result showed that the presence of z-VAD-FMK could effectively block the production of the smaller DIAP1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The knockdown of either effector caspase DrICE or DCP-1 mostly blocked the appearance of the smaller DIAP1
source: Consistent with the results in Figure 3C, the knockdown of either effector caspase DrICE or DCP-1 mostly blocked the appearance of the smaller DIAP1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: A smaller form of exogenously expressed DIAP1 was readily detected using anti-HA but not anti-myc antibody
source: As expected, a smaller form of exogenously expressed DIAP1 was readily detected using anti-HA but not anti-myc antibody (Figure 3E), showing that this smaller form of DIAP1 lost its N-terminal.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The smaller form of exogenously expressed DIAP1 lost its N-terminal
source: As expected, a smaller form of exogenously expressed DIAP1 was readily detected using anti-HA but not anti-myc antibody (Figure 3E), showing that this smaller form of DIAP1 lost its N-terminal.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the fact that the smaller form is detected by anti-HA (C-terminal tag) but not anti-myc (N-terminal tag)

claim: The smaller form of exogenously expressed DIAP1 accumulated during the course of viral infection, but was almost completely degraded at 24 h.p.i.
source: This smaller form of exogenously expressed DIAP1 accumulated during the course of viral infection, but was almost completely degraded at 24 h.p.i. (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: z-VAD-FMK blocked the generation of the smaller form of exogenously expressed DIAP1
source: Consistent with our previous data in Figure 3C, z-VAD-FMK blocked the generation of the smaller form of exogenously expressed DIAP1 (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: The production of the smaller form of DIAP1 was mediated by caspase cleavage
source: These data indicate that the production of the smaller form of DIAP1 was mediated by caspase cleavage.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing that caspase inhibition blocks the production of the smaller DIAP1 form

claim: The D20A mutation eliminated the appearance of the smaller form of DIAP1
source: Our data showed that the D20A mutation eliminated the appearance of the smaller form of DIAP1 (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: The M38A mutation failed to prevent the production of the smaller form of DIAP1
source: On the other hand, the other mutation, M38A, which blocks the internal initiation at the in-frame second ATG, failed to prevent the production of the smaller form of DIAP1, similarly with wild-type (WT) DIAP1 (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H

claim: The smaller form of DIAP1, DIAP1ΔN20, was able to inhibit virus-induced caspase activity as effective as DIAP1WT
source: Our data showed that the smaller form of DIAP1, DIAP1ΔN20, was also able to inhibit virus-induced caspase activity as effective as DIAP1WT (Figure 3I), indicating that this cleaved form of DIAP1 is still active.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I

claim: The cleaved form of DIAP1 is still active in blocking apoptosis
source: Our data showed that the smaller form of DIAP1, DIAP1ΔN20, was also able to inhibit virus-induced caspase activity as effective as DIAP1WT (Figure 3I), indicating that this cleaved form of DIAP1 is still active.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that DIAP1ΔN20 inhibits caspase activity

claim: Viral infection caused the accumulation of a caspase-cleaved, smaller form of DIAP1 in cultured Drosophila cells
source: In conclusion, our data show that viral infection caused the accumulation of a caspase-cleaved, smaller form of DIAP1, which is potent in apoptosis blockage, in cultured Drosophila cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3

claim: The caspase activity was enhanced after 12 h.p.i. of DCV
source: Interestingly, we observed that the caspase activity was enhanced after 12 h.p.i. (Figure 4A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The apparent accumulation of the smaller DIAP1 was readily detectable at 6 h.p.i.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the caspase activity was enhanced after 12 h.p.i. (Figure 4A), while the apparent accumulation of the smaller DIAP1 was readily detectable at 6 h.p.i. (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: At early stage of viral infection, the accumulation of smaller DIAP1 is not due to enhanced caspase activity
source: Thus, at least at early stage of viral infection, the accumulation of smaller DIAP1 is not due to enhanced caspase activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that smaller DIAP1 accumulates at 6 h.p.i. while caspase activity is enhanced only after 12 h.p.i.

claim: Knockdown of N-end rule pathway key component NTAN1 or ATE1 by RNAi resulted in the accumulation of caspase-cleaved, smaller DIAP1
source: Consistent with pervious study (Ditzel et al., 2003), knockdown of N-end rule pathway key component NTAN1 or ATE1 by RNAi resulted in the accumulation of caspase-cleaved, smaller DIAP1 (Figure 4C), confirming that the N-end rule pathway participates in the degradation of the caspase-cleaved DIAP1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and is consistent with a previous study cited (Ditzel et al., 2003)

claim: The N-end rule pathway participates in the degradation of the caspase-cleaved DIAP1
source: Consistent with pervious study (Ditzel et al., 2003), knockdown of N-end rule pathway key component NTAN1 or ATE1 by RNAi resulted in the accumulation of caspase-cleaved, smaller DIAP1 (Figure 4C), confirming that the N-end rule pathway participates in the degradation of the caspase-cleaved DIAP1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and is consistent with a previous study cited (Ditzel et al., 2003)

claim: Viral infection could induce the accumulation of smaller DIAP1 in cells expressing DIAP1WT from 0 (mock) to 15 h.p.i.
source: Our data show that although viral infection could induce the accumulation of smaller DIAP1 in cells expressing DIAP1WT from 0 (mock) to 15 h.p.i. (Figure 4D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The cleaved, smaller form of DIAP1 became resistant to degradation and insensitive to viral infection in DIAP1N21A-expressing cells
source: Our data show that although viral infection could induce the accumulation of smaller DIAP1 in cells expressing DIAP1WT from 0 (mock) to 15 h.p.i. (Figure 4D), the cleaved, smaller form of DIAP1 became resistant to degradation and insensitive to viral infection in DIAP1N21A-expressing cells (Figure 4E)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: The effect of viral infection on the smaller DIAP1 accumulation is dependent on the N-end rule pathway
source: Our data show that although viral infection could induce the accumulation of smaller DIAP1 in cells expressing DIAP1WT from 0 (mock) to 15 h.p.i. (Figure 4D), the cleaved, smaller form of DIAP1 became resistant to degradation and insensitive to viral infection in DIAP1N21A-expressing cells (Figure 4E), showing that the effect of viral infection on the smaller DIAP1 accumulation is dependent on the N-end rule pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that the N21A mutation makes DIAP1 insensitive to viral infection

claim: Viral infection did not increase the accumulation of the cleaved, smaller form of DIAP1N21D
source: Interestingly, viral infection did not increase the accumulation of the cleaved, smaller form of DIAP1N21D (Figure 4F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: The inhibition of the deamidation step of the N-end rule pathway is required for the virus-induced accumulation of cleaved DIAP1
source: Interestingly, viral infection did not increase the accumulation of the cleaved, smaller form of DIAP1N21D (Figure 4F), indicating that the inhibition of the deamidation step of the N-end rule pathway is required for the virus-induced accumulation of cleaved DIAP1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that the N21D mutation, which skips the deamidation step, prevents virus-induced accumulation of cleaved DIAP1

claim: Viral infection induced the gradual decrease of the protein level of NTAN1 but not ATE1
source: Consistent with our previous observation that the cleaved DIAP1 accumulation is dependent on the inhibition of NTAN1-mediated deamidation step (Figure 4F), our data show that viral infection induced the gradual decrease of the protein level of NTAN1 but not ATE1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The mRNA levels of NTAN1 and ATE1 are both up-regulated during the same time course of viral infection
source: Interestingly, the mRNA levels of NTAN1 and ATE1 are both up-regulated during the same time course of viral infection (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The exogenously expressed NTAN1 was down-regulated during the course of viral infection
source: In addition, we examined the effect of viral infection to exogenously expressed NTAN1 in cultured cells, and found that the exogenously expressed NTAN1 was also down-regulated during the course of viral infection (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The level of exogenously expressed EGFP was not affected by viral infection
source: On the other hand, the level of exogenously expressed EGFP was not affected by viral infection (Figure 5D), confirming that the protein expression using the same expression vector was not affected by viral infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Viral infection induced the decrease of NTAN1 protein level in a post-transcriptional manner
source: Together, these data indicate that viral infection induced the decrease of NTAN1 protein level in a post-transcriptional manner.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that NTAN1 protein decreases while NTAN1 mRNA increases during viral infection

claim: Viral infection immediately after CHX addition did not accelerate NTAN1 depletion
source: Similar with that of DIAP1, while viral infection immediately after CHX addition did not accelerate NTAN1 depletion (Figure 5E, lanes 1–2 vs. 3–4)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Viral infection before CHX addition significantly promoted NTAN1 degradation rate when compared with that in non-infected cells
source: Similar with that of DIAP1, while viral infection immediately after CHX addition did not accelerate NTAN1 depletion (Figure 5E, lanes 1–2 vs. 3–4), viral infection before CHX addition significantly promoted NTAN1 degradation rate when compared with that in non-infected cells (Figure 5E, lanes 1–2 vs. 5–6, Figure 5F,G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E, F, G and H

claim: Viral infection promoted the accumulation of NTAN1 after 12 h.p.i.
source: Interestingly, viral infection promoted the accumulation of NTAN1 after 12 h.p.i. (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Virus induced the degradation of NTAN1 protein in the early stage of infection
source: In conclusion, our data showed that virus induced the degradation of NTAN1 protein in the early stage of infection, which could lead to the accumulation of caspase cleaved, smaller form of DIAP1.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 5

claim: During viral infection, the NTAN1 protein levels could be restored by either MG-132 or lactacystin treatment
source: The results show that, during viral infection, the NTAN1 protein levels could be restored by either MG-132 or lactacystin treatment (Figure 6A and B), suggesting that the proteasome pathway is involved in virus-induced degradation of NTAN1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B

claim: The proteasome pathway is involved in virus-induced degradation of NTAN1
source: The results show that, during viral infection, the NTAN1 protein levels could be restored by either MG-132 or lactacystin treatment (Figure 6A and B), suggesting that the proteasome pathway is involved in virus-induced degradation of NTAN1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that proteasome inhibitors restore NTAN1 protein levels during viral infection

claim: Viral infection was able to induce the decrease of NTAN14KA protein level
source: However, when NTAN14KA was exogenously expressed in Drosophila S2 cells, viral infection was still able to induce the decrease of NTAN14KA protein level (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: In the absence of viral infection, NTAN14KA is significantly more stable than NTAN1WT
source: Furthermore, we conducted CHX degradation assay, and observed that in the absence of viral infection, NTAN14KA is significantly more stable than NTAN1WT, while viral infection similarly promoted the degradation of both NTAN14KA and NTAN1WT (Figure 6D–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D–H

claim: Viral infection similarly promoted the degradation of both NTAN14KA and NTAN1WT
source: Furthermore, we conducted CHX degradation assay, and observed that in the absence of viral infection, NTAN14KA is significantly more stable than NTAN1WT, while viral infection similarly promoted the degradation of both NTAN14KA and NTAN1WT (Figure 6D–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D–H

claim: The virus-induced NTAN1 degradation is independent of ubiquitylation
source: These results show that the virus-induced NTAN1 degradation is independent of ubiquitylation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that NTAN14KA, which cannot be ubiquitylated on lysine residues, is still degraded by viral infection

claim: Blocking the proteasome by MG-132 treatment did not show any effect on the protein level of NTAN14KA in the absence of viral infection
source: Interestingly, NTAN14KA is significantly more stable than NTAN1WT (Figures 6D, F and H); additionally, unlike NTAN1WT (Figure 6A, lanes 1 vs. 5), blocking the proteasome by MG-132 treatment did not show any effect on the protein level of NTAN14KA in the absence of viral infection (Figure 6C, lanes 1 vs. 4)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: NTAN1WT but not NTAN14KA can be polyubiquitylated
source: Moreover, our results showed that NTAN1WT but not NTAN14KA can be polyubiquitylated, while the polyubiquitylation of NTAN1 was not affected by viral infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A

claim: The polyubiquitylation of NTAN1 was not affected by viral infection
source: Moreover, our results showed that NTAN1WT but not NTAN14KA can be polyubiquitylated, while the polyubiquitylation of NTAN1 was not affected by viral infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A

claim: K186 is most responsible for the ubiquitylation-dependent degradation of NTAN1 in the absence of viral infection
source: On the other hand, like NTAN14KA, NTAN1K186A is resistant to degradation in the absence of viral infection (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2E, lanes 1 vs. 4), indicating that K186 is most responsible for the ubiquitylation-dependent degradation of NTAN1 in the absence of viral infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that NTAN1K186A is resistant to degradation in the absence of viral infection

claim: NTAN1 can be polyubiquitylated, and degraded by both ubiquitylation-dependent and -independent degradation pathways
source: Altogether, our data showed that NTAN1 can be polyubiquitylated, and degraded by both ubiquitylation-dependent and -independent degradation pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 6

claim: Both NTAN1 degradation pathways are dependent on proteasome
source: Altogether, our data showed that NTAN1 can be polyubiquitylated, and degraded by both ubiquitylation-dependent and -independent degradation pathways. While both NTAN1 degradation pathways are dependent on proteasome, the virus-induced NTAN1 degradation is independent of ubiquitylation (as illustrated in Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 6

claim: The virus-induced NTAN1 degradation is independent of ubiquitylation
source: Altogether, our data showed that NTAN1 can be polyubiquitylated, and degraded by both ubiquitylation-dependent and -independent degradation pathways. While both NTAN1 degradation pathways are dependent on proteasome, the virus-induced NTAN1 degradation is independent of ubiquitylation (as illustrated in Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 6

claim: The ectopic expression of HA-NTAN1 partially restored the expression of NTAN1, resulting in the almost elimination of both full-length and caspase-cleaved forms of DIAP1 at 15 and 18 h.p.i.
source: Our results showed that the ectopic expression of HA-NTAN1 partially restored the expression of NTAN1, resulting in the almost elimination of both full-length and caspase-cleaved forms of DIAP1 at 15 and 18 h.p.i. (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: In the context of viral infection, the partial restoration of NTAN1 expression significantly promoted apoptosis
source: Consequently, in the context of viral infection, the partial restoration of NTAN1 expression significantly promoted apoptosis (Figure 7B) and the relative caspase activity in cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: In the context of viral infection, the partial restoration of NTAN1 expression significantly promoted the relative caspase activity in cells
source: Consequently, in the context of viral infection, the partial restoration of NTAN1 expression significantly promoted apoptosis (Figure 7B) and the relative caspase activity in cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: The partial restoration of NTAN1 expression significantly restricted viral RNA replication at 18 h.p.i.
source: Furthermore, the partial restoration of NTAN1 expression also significantly restricted viral RNA replication at 18 h.p.i. (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D

claim: The knockdown of NTAN1 inhibited virus-induced apoptosis and enhanced DCV replication
source: Moreover, the knockdown of NTAN1 inhibited virus-induced apoptosis and enhanced DCV replication (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Virus-induced NTAN1 degradation can inhibit apoptosis and benefit viral replication
source: Altogether, these data indicate that virus-induced NTAN1 degradation can inhibit apoptosis and benefit viral replication.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 7

claim: A picorna-like virus can induce apoptosis
source: In this study, we demonstrate that a picorna-like virus can induce apoptosis, and the virus-induced apoptosis plays an antiviral role in Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the Results section

claim: The virus-induced apoptosis plays an antiviral role in Drosophila
source: In this study, we demonstrate that a picorna-like virus can induce apoptosis, and the virus-induced apoptosis plays an antiviral role in Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the Results section

claim: Viral infection is able to induce the degradation of NTAN1 via an ubiquitylation-independent proteasome pathway in cells
source: Strikingly, we uncovered that viral infection is able to induce the degradation of NTAN1, a key component of the N-end rule degradation pathway, via an ubiquitylation-independent proteasome pathway in cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the Results section

claim: The virus-induced degradation of NTAN1 caused the accumulation of caspase-cleaved, shorter form of DIAP1 by inhibiting its N-terminal Asn deamidation
source: The virus-induced degradation of NTAN1 caused the accumulation of caspase-cleaved, shorter form of DIAP1 by inhibiting its N-terminal Asn deamidation, resulting in the suppression of apoptosis and the enhancement of viral replication (as illustrated in Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 8

claim: The virus-induced N-end rule pathway suppression results in the suppression of apoptosis and the enhancement of viral replication
source: The virus-induced degradation of NTAN1 caused the accumulation of caspase-cleaved, shorter form of DIAP1 by inhibiting its N-terminal Asn deamidation, resulting in the suppression of apoptosis and the enhancement of viral replication (as illustrated in Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 8

claim: The apoptotic pathway is recognized as an antiviral defense mechanism
source: The apoptotic pathway is recognized as an antiviral defense mechanism (Everett and McFadden, 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Everett and McFadden, 1999

claim: The infection by a picorna-like virus can suppress the N-end rule pathway by inducing the degradation of its key component NTAN1
source: Our current study uncovered that the infection by a picorna-like virus can suppress the N-end rule pathway by inducing the degradation of its key component NTAN1.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the Results section

claim: The virus-induced suppression of the N-end rule pathway causes the accumulation of caspase-cleaved DIAP1, which results in apoptosis inhibition
source: This process causes the accumulation of caspase-cleaved DIAP1, which results in apoptosis inhibition and represents a novel mechanism of viral evasion of apoptosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the Results section

claim: The virus-induced degradation of NTAN1 is dependent of proteasome but independent of ubiquitylation
source: It is interesting that the virus-induced degradation of NTAN1 is dependent of proteasome but independent of ubiquitylation (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: The ubiquitin-independent proteolytic activity of proteasomes is involved in the degradation of oxidized proteins, chemically unfolded proteins, and specific natively disordered proteins
source: It has been reported that the ubiquitin-independent proteolytic activity of proteasomes is involved in the degradation of oxidized proteins, chemically unfolded proteins, and specific natively disordered proteins (Baugh et al., 2009; Grune et al., 2003; Hoyt and Coffino, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baugh et al., 2009; Grune et al., 2003; Hoyt and Coffino, 2004

claim: Several important regulatory proteins can be degraded by ubiquitin-independent proteasome mechanism
source: It is worth to mention that several important regulatory proteins can be degraded by this mechanism (Hoyt and Coffino, 2004), including p21/Cip1 (Sheaff et al., 2000), IκBα (Krappmann et al., 1996), c-Jun (Jariel-Encontre et al., 1995) and p53 (Tsvetkov et al., 2009; Tsvetkov et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The N-end rule pathway is normally recognized as an ubiquitin proteasome proteolytic system and employs specific E3 ubiquitin ligases
source: The N-end rule pathway is normally recognized as an ubiquitin proteasome proteolytic system and employs specific E3 ubiquitin ligases.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the N-end rule pathway

claim: NTAN1 can be degraded in an ubiquitin-independent manner
source: As a key component of the N-end rule pathway, NTAN1 can be degraded in an ubiquitin-independent manner suggests a connection between these distinct proteasome proteolytic mechanisms
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 6

claim: The N-end rule pathway plays an important role in various biological processes
source: The N-end rule pathway plays an important role in various biological processes.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the N-end rule pathway

claim: NTAN1 is the key component that regulates the half-life of a protein by identifying its N-terminal residue and initiating the process
source: In the N-end rule pathway, NTAN1 is the key component that regulates the half-life of a protein by identifying its N-terminal residue and initiating the process.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about NTAN1's role in the N-end rule pathway

claim: NTAN1-deficient mice have neurological defects such as impairment of spontaneous activity and spatial memory
source: It has been reported that NTAN1-deficient mice have neurological defects such as impairment of spontaneous activity and spatial memory (Balogh et al., 2000, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Balogh et al., 2000, 2001

claim: Viral infection can induce NTAN1 degradation, resulting in the suppression of the N-end rule pathway and subsequent evasion of apoptosis
source: Our current study found that viral infection can induce NTAN1 degradation, resulting in the suppression of the N-end rule pathway and subsequent evasion of apoptosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the Results section

claim: Blocking protein synthesis by CHX before viral infection abolished the effect of DCV to induce NTAN1 degradation
source: Interestingly, we found that blocking protein synthesis by CHX before viral infection abolished the effect of DCV to induce NTAN1 degradation, indicating that viral protein synthesis and/or viral replication within infected cells, but not the input viral components, are responsible for this process.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from CHX degradation assays

claim: Viral protein synthesis and/or viral replication within infected cells, but not the input viral components, are responsible for NTAN1 degradation
source: Interestingly, we found that blocking protein synthesis by CHX before viral infection abolished the effect of DCV to induce NTAN1 degradation, indicating that viral protein synthesis and/or viral replication within infected cells, but not the input viral components, are responsible for this process.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that blocking protein synthesis abolishes NTAN1 degradation
